title: Venous leg ulcer
summary: The commonest chronic leg ulcer: a shallow, sloping, exudative ulcer in the gaiter area. Compression after ABPI is the cornerstone. Colonised does not mean infected.

glance.think: A shallow, sloping, wet ulcer over the medial malleolus with haemosiderin staining, venous eczema, varicose veins and oedema that is worse at the end of the day.
glance.engine: Venous hypertension from incompetent valves, previous DVT or calf-pump failure, causing oedema, inflammation and skin breakdown.
glance.backbone: ABPI, then multilayer compression, elevation, walking, emollient, and lifelong stockings after healing.
glance.never_miss: Arterial disease before compressing, and a non-healing or atypical ulcer (malignancy, PG, vasculitis).

what: A venous leg ulcer is full-thickness skin loss caused by **chronic venous insufficiency** (venous hypertension). It is the **most common** chronic leg ulcer. Other names are stasis ulcer and gravitational ulcer. Avoid calling it a ‘varicose ulcer’ if there are no varicose veins.

list: **Valve incompetence**, previous **DVT**, obesity, immobility and calf-muscle pump failure cause **venous hypertension**.
This leads to oedema, haemosiderin deposition, inflammation and lipodermatosclerosis, with poor oxygen and nutrient delivery.
The skin then breaks down after **minor trauma** and fails to heal.
**Gaiter area**, most commonly over the **medial malleolus**.
Surrounding skin: varicose veins, brown **haemosiderin** staining, **venous eczema**, atrophie blanche, and **lipodermatosclerosis** (the ‘inverted champagne bottle’ leg).
**Dependent oedema**, worse when the leg is down.
Pain is usually milder than with arterial ulcers, unless the ulcer is infected.
Clinical, with signs of venous disease.
**ABPI** (ankle–brachial pressure index) **before any high compression**, to exclude significant arterial disease.
Venous duplex if intervention is planned.
Swab **only** if there are clinical signs of infection.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Punched-out, distal (toes, pressure points), claudication or rest pain, cold foot, weak pulses, **low ABPI**
Plantar pressure points, **painless**, callus, diabetes with neuropathy
Rapid, very painful, **violaceous undermined edge**; pathergy
Atypical site or edge, rolled or raised margin, non-healing. **Biopsy or refer**
Over a bony prominence in an immobile patient

differentials: See also: [arterial ulcers](condition:arterial-leg-ulcer) and [diabetic foot ulcers](condition:diabetic-foot-ulcer) · [Pyoderma gangrenosum](condition:pyoderma-gangrenosum)
management: Based on NICE CG168 and local leg ulcer and tissue viability pathways.

list: **Compression** (multilayer bandaging or hosiery) is the cornerstone, **once ABPI is satisfactory**.
Leg elevation, walking and ankle exercises, weight management, and emollients.
Treat **venous eczema** with short courses of mild to potent topical steroid around (not in) the ulcer.
Wound care: moist healing and debridement by tissue viability. Do not use topical antibiotics routinely.
**Infection:** give systemic antibiotics **only** for spreading cellulitis or systemic signs. Colonisation is not infection.
Pentoxifylline is sometimes used as an adjunct, following specialist or local policy.

management: To vascular surgery, tissue viability or dermatology if: not healing after about 2 weeks of optimal care, atypical appearance, mixed arterial disease, or for venous intervention (NICE: refer for venous assessment).
red_flags: **Low or abnormal ABPI**, absent pulses, rest pain or a cold foot: arterial disease, so **do not compress**. Refer to vascular.
Spreading redness, fever or systemic upset: cellulitis or sepsis.
Rolled, raised or irregular edge, bleeding, or failure to heal: biopsy to exclude **SCC or BCC** (Marjolin ulcer).
Rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a purple edge: suspect **pyoderma gangrenosum**.
pearls: **Never start high compression without a vascular assessment or ABPI.**
Explain **lifelong compression stockings** after healing, because recurrence is common.
Good analgesia and exudate control improve adherence to compression.
Topical steroids on surrounding venous eczema help. Watch for contact allergy to dressings and topical products, which is common in leg ulcer patients.
